title: Practical Non-Stationary Graph Gaussian Processes
claim: A single learned exponent continuously interpolates between amplifying and suppressing interactions of high-variability nodes, recovering stationary correlations at one special value.
layout: 2x4 grid of graph panels, left-to-right sweep, red boxes highlight special cases
description: A 2×4 grid of small panels, each showing the same nine-node ring graph with a few chords. Orange nodes mark high-variability nodes and blue nodes mark baseline nodes. Columns are titled by the coupling exponent γ = −1 (propagation), 0 (uniform coupling), +1 (stationary) and +2 (isolation). The top row shows precision magnitude |Q_ij| in gray edges. Edges touching orange nodes are very thick at γ=−1 and fade to thin at γ=+2. The bottom row shows correlation deviation from the stationary baseline in red edges. These are thick at the extremes, thin at γ=0, and almost invisible at γ=+1. Red boxes with labels highlight the uniform case (γ=0, top) and the zero-deviation case (γ=+1, bottom). A legend at the bottom explains the node colors. The eye goes first to the thick edges and the red boxes.
caption: One learned $\gamma$ selects propagation or isolation. Orange nodes have high $d_i$; blue nodes are baseline. Edge thickness shows $|\m{Q}_{ij}|$ (top) and correlation deviation from the stationary baseline (bottom). For high-$d_i$ nodes, $\gamma<0$ amplifies coupling and $\gamma>0$ suppresses it. Highlighted: $\gamma=0$, uniform coupling; $\gamma=1$, stationary correlations with node-dependent variances.
abstract: Gaussian processes on graphs provide a principled framework for prediction and uncertainty estimation, but modelling heterogeneous networks often requires balancing flexibility against parameter complexity. Variability at a node may reflect useful signal that should propagate through the network, unreliable measurements whose influence should be suppressed, or a mixture of both. We introduce Variance-Coupled Gaussian Processes (VCGPs), which use a positive auxiliary signal to modulate graph interactions through a single learned coupling exponent. The exponent controls how strongly high-variability nodes propagate or attenuate information, while a cluster-wise extension accommodates different regimes within the same graph. Under stated structural assumptions, we characterize the unique stationary-rescaling point of the basic family, where correlations match those of a stationary graph kernel while node-dependent variances remain. Experiments on traffic, air-quality and weather datasets show competitive prediction and uncertainty estimation relative to stationary and per-node non-stationary baselines, with the largest gains on networks requiring multiple coupling regimes. Stationary correlations after variance rescaling remain sufficient on some data, and performance depends on the auxiliary signal and model selection.
